issues.legal_issue: A summary ejectment authority may act only when the statutory condition that the occupant is not entitled to use and occupy the land is established.
material_facts: Tenants alleged that they had been forcibly dispossessed of land and sought restoration through a summary ejectment proceeding.
The authorities ordered restoration on the basis that the current occupant was in wrongful or unauthorised possession.
No provision was identified that made the current occupant ineligible to use and occupy the land under the governing law.
issues.conclusion: The condition conferring jurisdiction on the Collector was absent, so the revenue authorities had no power to order ejectment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43(1)(b) of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Act, 1953 permits ejectment only where the person in wrongful or unauthorised possession is also not entitled to use and occupy the land under the Act. That entitlement condition is a prerequisite to the Collector’s jurisdiction. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.summary_ejectment_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding seeking ejectment through a summary authority.
predicates.occupant_alleged_wrongful_possession: A claimant alleges that the person occupying the land is in wrongful or unauthorised possession.
predicates.no_legal_disqualification_established: No basis is established for treating the occupant as ineligible under the governing law to use and occupy the land.

issues.definition: When a summary ejectment proceeding rests on an allegation of wrongful possession but no legal disqualification from occupying the land is established, the summary authority lacks ejectment jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A summary proceeding before an authority exercising judicial powers requires judicial determination of the facts that confer jurisdiction, rather than subjective satisfaction alone.
material_facts: The Collector conducted a summary proceeding to consider whether the occupant was in wrongful or unauthorised possession.
The Commissioner considered that the Collector could order ejectment on subjective satisfaction of wrongful or unauthorised possession.
The Supreme Court characterised the Collector’s proceeding as judicial and required determination of the facts that invested the Collector with jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The Collector had to determine judicially the facts that conferred jurisdiction and could not rely on subjective satisfaction alone.
issues.legal_principle: The Collector’s proceedings under Section 43 of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Act, 1953 are judicial in character despite being summary. The authority must judicially determine the facts that invest it with jurisdiction. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.summary_judicial_proceeding: The proceeding is summary but is conducted by an authority exercising judicial powers.
predicates.authority_power_depends_on_jurisdictiona: The authority’s power to grant the requested relief depends on whether specified facts exist.

issues.definition: When a summary judicial proceeding depends on specified facts for the authority’s power, the authority must determine those facts judicially.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory ejectment provision does not apply retrospectively to dispossession that occurred before the provision came into force.
material_facts: The tenants alleged that their dispossession occurred before the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Act, 1953 came into force.
They sought restoration under the Act after it came into force.
The High Court held that the provision had no retrospective operation, and the Supreme Court agreed.
issues.conclusion: The relevant ejectment provision had no retrospective operation and could not apply to the earlier dispossession.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of Section 43(1)(b) of the Pepsu Tenancy and Agricultural Act, 1953 do not give it retrospective operation. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.statutory_ejectment_proceeding: The proceeding seeks relief under a statutory ejectment provision.
predicates.claim_based_on_pre_commencement_disposse: The requested relief is based on a dispossession that occurred before the relevant provision came into force.

issues.definition: When statutory ejectment relief is sought on the basis of a dispossession predating the provision, the provision does not apply retrospectively.

issues.legal_issue: An order made without jurisdiction cannot be upheld merely because another authority could have granted similar relief or because the order was considered to achieve substantial justice.
material_facts: The Collector ordered restoration despite lacking the jurisdictional condition required for that order.
The State argued that the orders should stand because the authorities had done substantial justice and another authority might have granted the tenants similar relief.
The Court rejected that argument, holding that judicial or quasi-judicial authorities must act within their jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The orders could not be sustained on the ground that substantial justice had been done or that another authority might have granted the same relief.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial and quasi-judicial authorities may exercise their powers only within the limits of their jurisdiction. An order made without jurisdiction cannot be sustained merely because another authority, if lawfully approached, might have granted the relief. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: order_challenged_in_review and judicial_or_quasi_judicial_authority and authority_lacked_jurisdiction and similar_relief_possible_elsewhere

predicates.order_challenged_in_review: A party challenges an authority’s order in a review proceeding.
predicates.judicial_or_quasi_judicial_authority: The order was made by an authority exercising judicial or quasi-judicial powers.
predicates.authority_lacked_jurisdiction: The authority did not have jurisdiction to make the order.
predicates.similar_relief_possible_elsewhere: Another authority might have granted similar relief if properly approached.

issues.definition: When a judicial or quasi-judicial order is challenged in review, the authority lacked jurisdiction, and similar relief might have been available elsewhere, the order cannot be saved by substantial justice.
